{{short description|Derived graph of higher chromatic number}}

In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] area of [[graph theory]], the '''Mycielskian''' or '''Mycielski graph''' of an [[undirected graph]] is a larger graph formed from it by a construction of {{harvs|first=Jan|last=Mycielski|authorlink=Jan Mycielski|year=1955|txt}}. The construction preserves the property of being [[triangle-free graph|triangle-free]] but increases the [[chromatic number]]; by applying the construction repeatedly to a triangle-free starting graph, Mycielski showed that there exist triangle-free graphs with arbitrarily large chromatic number.

==Construction==
[[Image:Grötzsch graph as a Mycielskian.svg|thumb|360px|Mycielskian construction applied to a 5-[[cycle graph]], producing the [[Grötzsch graph]] with 11 vertices and 20 edges, the smallest triangle-free 4-chromatic graph {{harv|Chvátal|1974}}.]]
Let the ''n'' vertices of the given graph ''G'' be ''v''<sub>1</sub>, ''v''<sub>2</sub>, . . . , ''v''<sub>n</sub>. The Mycielski graph μ(''G'') contains ''G'' itself as a subgraph, together with ''n''+1 additional vertices: a vertex ''u''<sub>''i''</sub> corresponding to each vertex ''v''<sub>''i''</sub> of ''G'', and an extra vertex ''w''.  Each vertex ''u''<sub>''i''</sub> is connected by an edge to ''w'', so that these vertices form a subgraph in the form of a star ''K''<sub>1,''n''</sub>. In addition, for each edge ''v''<sub>''i''</sub>''v''<sub>''j''</sub> of ''G'', the Mycielski graph includes two edges, ''u''<sub>''i''</sub>''v''<sub>''j''</sub> and ''v''<sub>''i''</sub>''u''<sub>''j''</sub>.

Thus, if ''G'' has ''n'' vertices and ''m'' edges, μ(''G'') has 2''n''+1 vertices and 3''m''+''n'' edges. 

The only new triangles in μ(''G'') are of the form ''v''<sub>''i''</sub>''v''<sub>''j''</sub>''u''<sub>''k''</sub>, where ''v''<sub>''i''</sub>''v''<sub>''j''</sub>''v''<sub>''k''</sub> is a triangle  in ''G''. Thus, if ''G'' is triangle-free, so is μ(''G'').

To see that the construction increases the chromatic number <math>\chi(G)=k</math>, consider a proper ''k''-coloring of <math>\mu(G){-}\{w\}</math>; that is, a mapping <math>c : \{v_1,\ldots,v_n,u_1,\ldots,u_n\}\to \{1,2,\ldots,k\}</math> with <math>c(x)\neq c(y)</math> for adjacent vertices ''x'',''y''. If we had <math>c(u_i)\in \{1,2,\ldots,k{-}1\}</math> for all ''i'', then we could define a proper (''k''&minus;1)-coloring of ''G'' by <math>c'\!(v_i) = c(u_i)</math> when  <math>c(v_i) = k</math>, and <math>c'\!(v_i) = c(v_i)</math> otherwise. But this is impossible for <math>\chi(G)=k</math>, so ''c'' must use all ''k'' colors for <math>\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}</math>, and any proper coloring of the last vertex ''w'' must use an extra color. That is, <math>\chi(\mu(G))=k{+}1</math>.

==Iterated Mycielskians==
[[Image:Mycielski graphs.svg|thumb|360px|''M''<sub>2</sub>, ''M''<sub>3</sub> and ''M''<sub>4</sub> Mycielski graphs]]
Applying the Mycielskian repeatedly, starting with the one-edge graph, produces a sequence of graphs ''M''<sub>''i''</sub> = μ(''M''<sub>''i''&minus;1</sub>), sometimes called the Mycielski graphs. The first few graphs in this sequence are the graph ''M''<sub>2</sub> = ''K''<sub>2</sub> with two vertices connected by an edge, the [[cycle graph]] ''M''<sub>3</sub> = ''C''<sub>5</sub>, and the [[Grötzsch graph]] ''M''<sub>4</sub> with 11 vertices and 20 edges.

In general, the graph ''M''<sub>''i''</sub> is [[triangle-free graph|triangle-free]], (''i''&minus;1)-[[K-vertex-connected graph|vertex-connected]], and ''i''-[[chromatic number|chromatic]]. The number of vertices in ''M''<sub>''i''</sub> for ''i'' &ge; 2 is 3&nbsp;×&nbsp;2<sup>''i''&minus;2</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 {{OEIS|id=A083329}}, while the number of edges for ''i ≥ 2'' is <math>\frac{1}{2}\left(7 \times 3^{i-2} + 1\right) - 3 \times 2^{i-2}</math>, which begins as: 

: 1, 5, 20, 71, 236, 755, 2360, 7271, 22196, 67355, ... {{OEIS|id=A122695}}.

==Properties==
[[Image:Mycielski graph k4 hamiltonian path.svg|thumb|150px|Hamiltonian cycle in ''M''<sub>4</sub> (Grötzsch graph)]]
*If ''G'' has [[chromatic number]] ''k'', then μ(''G'') has chromatic number ''k''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 {{harv|Mycielski|1955}}.
*If ''G'' is [[triangle-free graph|triangle-free]], then so is μ(''G'') {{harv|Mycielski|1955}}.
*More generally, if ''G'' has [[clique number]] ω(''G''), then μ(''G'') has clique number of the maximum among 2 and ω(''G''). {{harv|Mycielski|1955}}
*If ''G'' is a [[factor-critical graph]], then so is μ(''G'') {{harv|Došlić|2005}}. In particular, every graph ''M''<sub>''i''</sub> for ''i''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;2 is factor-critical.
*If ''G'' has a [[Hamiltonian cycle]], then so does μ(''G'') {{harv|Fisher|McKenna|Boyer|1998}}.
*If ''G'' has [[domination number]] γ(''G''), then μ(''G'') has domination number γ(''G'')+1 {{harv|Fisher|McKenna|Boyer|1998}}.

==Cones over graphs==
[[File:Generalized Mycielskian.svg|thumb|A generalized Mycielskian, formed as a cone over the 5-cycle, Δ<sub>3</sub>(C<sub>5</sub>) = Δ<sub>3</sub>(Δ<sub>2</sub>(''K''<sub>2</sub>)).]]
A generalization of the Mycielskian, called a cone over a graph, was introduced by {{harvtxt|Stiebitz|1985}} and further studied by {{harvtxt|Tardif|2001}} and {{harvtxt|Lin|Wu|Lam|Gu|2006}}. In this construction, one forms a graph <math>\Delta_i(G)</math> from a given graph ''G'' by taking the [[Tensor product of graphs|tensor product]] ''G''&nbsp;×&nbsp;''H'', where ''H'' is a path of length ''i'' with a self-loop at one end, and then collapsing into a single supervertex all of the vertices associated with the vertex of ''H'' at the non-loop end of the path. The Mycielskian itself can be formed in this way as μ(''G'') = Δ<sub>2</sub>(''G'').

While the cone construction does not always increase the chromatic number, {{harvtxt|Stiebitz|1985}} proved that it does so when applied iteratively to ''K''<sub>2</sub>. That is, define a sequence of families of graphs, called generalized Mycielskians, as
: ℳ(2) = {''K''<sub>2</sub>} and ℳ(''k''+1) = {<math>\Delta_i(G)</math> | ''G'' ∈ ℳ(''k''), i ∈ <math>\mathbb{N}</math>}.
For example, ℳ(3) is the family of odd cycles. Then each graph in ℳ(''k'') is ''k''-chromatic. The proof uses methods of [[topological combinatorics]] developed by [[László Lovász]] to compute the chromatic number of [[Kneser graph]]s.
The triangle-free property is then strengthened as follows: if one only applies the cone construction Δ<sub>''i''</sub> for ''i'' ≥ ''r'', then the resulting graph has [[odd girth]] at least 2''r'' + 1, that is, it contains no odd cycles of length less than 2''r'' + 1.
Thus generalized Mycielskians provide a simple construction of graphs with high chromatic number and high odd girth.
